rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 and Figure 6 - the authors collect their own UAV RGB images from three olive fields in northern Greece (429 images, 160 tiles, 3038 annotated instances), train three YOLOv5 architectures and report precision, recall and mAP on a held-out test set.
rows.notes: The study reports its own data but not evidence for the claimed effect. It shows that YOLOv5 applied to UAV RGB imagery can detect olive trees and classify them as healthy or damaged by Verticillium wilt, with the medium model at 640x640 performing best (Figure 6). It does not concern Xylella fastidiosa, the pathogen the claim is about; it does not demonstrate control of disease spread (detection only); and it does not demonstrate early detection before symptoms are visible to the human eye - images were taken in October-November when symptoms are most pronounced, damaged trees were labelled by experts on visibly altered colour (Section 4), and early detection via thermal/NIR imagery is explicitly listed as future work (Section 6). Detection is at best a precondition of control, so upstream is set to true. Technology (UAV remote sensing) broadly matches the passage, so no technology mismatch is flagged, although the pathogen differs. Results are single values per model with no dispersion measures; limitations noted are about class imbalance and few training images, not about the claimed control effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a methods/computer-vision paper on detecting Verticillium-damaged olive trees from UAV RGB imagery; the review cites it in the context of Xylella fastidiosa control and early detection, which the study does not address.
